title: Two orchestras sing the last lament
work: Symphony No. 6 in B minor “Pathétique”, Op. 74 — IV. Finale: Adagio lamentoso
question: How do two orchestras keep Tchaikovsky’s slow finale moving as its melodies fall towards silence?
intro: In February 1893, Tchaikovsky told his nephew Vladimir Davydov that his new symphony would end with “a most long-drawn-out Adagio”. The finale begins with a falling melody whose notes pass between the two violin sections. Furtwängler’s Berlin Philharmonic and the Musopen Symphony carry that lament through its great outbursts to the quiet low strings at the end.

recordings.label: Wilhelm Furtwängler, Berlin Philharmonic
recordings.note: Broad phrases keep their momentum through the lament; Furtwängler draws the climaxes into long sweeps.

recordings.label: Musopen Symphony
recordings.note: The modern recording carries the whole finale, from the opening violin exchanges to the last descent into cellos and basses.

passages.label: One tune, two violin sections
passages.note: First and second violins exchange notes of the falling tune. Together they make a melody that neither section plays complete.

passages.label: The D-major song
passages.note: Horns support a broad descending melody in the first violins and violas; trombones answer it.

passages.label: The orchestra rushes down
passages.note: Fast descending scales carry the broad melody to its climax. The whole orchestra joins the fall.

passages.label: Brass joins the lament
passages.note: The returning lament reaches another outburst. Trombones and tuba reinforce the strings as the music presses towards a long-held F♯.

passages.label: The last descent
passages.note: The broad melody returns in B minor. Muted strings descend, and the tune sinks gradually towards the cellos and basses.

alignment.timeBasis: Absolute seconds in each supplied stream; trim ends are exclusive.
